article_title: Agentic AI-driven Immersive Simulation: A Knowledge-Aware Virtual Training Platform for High Dose Rate (HDR) Brachytherapy
citation: Ronghua Xu, Kepha Barasa, Manoj Kumal, Xinyun Liu, Weihua Zhou, Xin Qian. (2026). Agentic AI-driven Immersive Simulation: A Knowledge-Aware Virtual Training Platform for High Dose Rate (HDR) Brachytherapy. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08163
title: HDR VC brachytherapy immersive VR training platform with hands-free voice assistant
description: A distributed edge-cloud system pairing a Meta Quest 3 VR frontend with a GPU-accelerated backend. The frontend renders "a high-fidelity digital twin of an HDR brachytherapy suite" with anatomically precise patient models, catheters, afterloaders, and applicators, and a three-tier voice interface (STT, TTS, diegetic virtual monitors) that removes controller dependency during procedures. The article positions it as risk-free, repeatable pre-training that complements physical HDR training.
requirements: A VR headset with microphone array and a dedicated backend server for LLM inference and vector retrieval, connected via asynchronous RESTful APIs
constraints: The system remains partially dependent on Meta's SDK evolution and hardware/software support lifecycle, mitigated by a modular architecture decoupling the VR interface layer
Current VR technology cannot track users' hand movements, so the system provides no automated assessment of procedural correctness
target_learning_goals: mastering HDR vaginal cylinder brachytherapy procedures
spatial reasoning about applicator placement relative to organs at risk
examples: Prototype tested on Meta Quest 3 and Quest Pro with trainees interacting with a 3D HDR afterloader, plugging in or detaching applicator cables, and querying a virtual AI assistant in the control room
key_sources: Ronghua Xu, Kepha Barasa, Manoj Kumal, Xinyun Liu, Weihua Zhou, Xin Qian. (2026). Agentic AI-driven Immersive Simulation: A Knowledge-Aware Virtual Training Platform for High Dose Rate (HDR) Brachytherapy. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08163

article_title: Implementation of a Hypothesis-Driven Physical Exam Session in a Transition to Clerkship Program.
citation: Kelly J, Oza SK, Feinn R, Cassese T. (2020). Implementation of a Hypothesis-Driven Physical Exam Session in a Transition to Clerkship Program. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11043
title: Hypothesis-driven physical exam workshop pattern: vignette-based differential diagnosis generation, maneuver selection with justification, and supervised peer practice
description: This lesson-level pattern organizes a clinical-skills workshop around five clinical vignettes. For each vignette, students "worked in pairs to brainstorm differential diagnoses, determine the relevant HDPE maneuvers to perform, and establish a rationale for performing each maneuver," then joined a facilitator-led small-group discussion on diagnostic approach, indicated maneuvers, and expected findings, and finally practiced selected maneuvers in pairs while the facilitator circulated with feedback. A student worksheet structures differential generation and maneuver justification, and a facilitator guide supplies suggested diagnoses, maneuvers, and rationale.
requirements: A facilitator preparation session reviewing goals, format, and small-group facilitation
A student worksheet with differential prompts and maneuver-justification tables
A facilitator guide with suggested diagnoses, maneuvers, rationale, and timeline
One facilitator per nine to 10 students for direct observation and feedback
constraints: Requires facilitator availability and adequate classroom/clinical skills facility space
Developed at a single institution, which could limit generalizability to institutions with different curricular structures
target_learners: Rising third-year medical students entering clerkships
target_learning_goals: Generate a differential diagnosis from a case vignette
Select and justify physical exam maneuvers based on the differential
Perform focused PE maneuvers with proper technique
examples: In June 2019, 192 rising third-year students worked in groups of nine to 10 per facilitator through five clerkship-representative vignettes over a 3-hour session
key_sources: Kelly J, Oza SK, Feinn R, Cassese T. (2020). Implementation of a Hypothesis-Driven Physical Exam Session in a Transition to Clerkship Program. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11043

article_title: Implementation of a Hypothesis-Driven Physical Exam Session in a Transition to Clerkship Program.
citation: Kelly J, Oza SK, Feinn R, Cassese T. (2020). Implementation of a Hypothesis-Driven Physical Exam Session in a Transition to Clerkship Program. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11043
title: HDPE session instructional materials: student worksheet, facilitator guide, and survey appendices
description: The session's released materials comprise a student worksheet, a facilitator guide, and survey instruments, all peer reviewed as integral parts of the publication. The worksheet "included a prompt for generating differential diagnoses and a table into which students entered their brainstormed HDPE maneuvers and justified the choice of each maneuver," followed by text and visual demonstrations of normal exam technique and findings. The facilitator guide adds "a suggested time line for the session, suggested differential diagnoses and potential approaches to each chief complaint, suggested PE maneuvers with rationale, and a proposed wrap-up section."
requirements: Facilitator training reviewing session goals, format, and small-group facilitation suggestions
constraints: The intended electronic real-time worksheet data collection failed due to internet connectivity problems, so worksheet data were excluded from analyses
target_learners: Rising third-year medical students and the physician facilitators who lead their small groups
target_learning_goals: Generate and justify differential-diagnosis-driven physical exam maneuver selection
examples: Five case vignettes developed by faculty educators and chosen to represent cases from the institution's core clerkships
key_sources: Kelly J, Oza SK, Feinn R, Cassese T. (2020). Implementation of a Hypothesis-Driven Physical Exam Session in a Transition to Clerkship Program. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11043
